title: AI Governance Checklist
subtitle: Twelve controls to build, run and evidence responsible AI at enterprise scale.
mapping_note: Framework references are indicative mappings to help you find the relevant requirement. "Also maps to" covers ISO/IEC 27090:2026 (AI security), EN 18286:2026 (the EU AI Act harmonised quality-management standard), IEEE 2863-2026 (organisational AI governance) and Australia's Guidance for AI Adoption (AI6). Verify against the current official text of each standard or law before relying on them for compliance.

items.description: Identify and record every AI system, model, tool, agent and use case in the organisation, including embedded vendor AI and shadow use.
items.evidence: AI register with owner, purpose, data used, vendor, risk tier and lifecycle status for each entry; date of last review.
items.test: Pick three business units at random. Does every AI tool they use appear in the register?
items.owner: Chief AI Officer / AI governance lead

items.description: Apply one consistent method to rate AI risk by impact and likelihood, and tie each tier to the controls and approvals it requires.
items.evidence: Approved risk methodology; risk tier recorded against every register entry; documented tier-to-control matrix.
items.test: Can two assessors rate the same use case independently and land on the same tier?
items.more: EN 18286:2026 (Art. 17(1)(g) risk management within the QMS); Australia AI6 practices 2–3 (impacts, risk)

items.description: Stand up a cross-functional AI governance body with clear terms of reference, decision rights and a named accountable owner for every AI system.
items.evidence: Terms of reference; membership spanning risk, legal, privacy, security, data and business; minutes showing decisions made.
items.test: For any production AI system, can you name the one person accountable for it in under a minute?
items.more: IEEE 2863-2026 (governance principles and processes for the governing body); Australia AI6 practice 1 (accountability)

items.description: Approve and publish policies covering ethics, acceptable use, data, model governance and accountability, and train people on them.
items.evidence: Board- or executive-approved AI policy; review date; staff attestation or training completion records.
items.test: Ask five staff where the AI policy lives and what it forbids. How many can answer?
items.more: EN 18286:2026 (harmonised QMS standard for Art. 17; presumption of conformity from 14 Oct 2026); IEEE 2863-2026

items.description: Use standard templates such as model cards and datasheets so every system can be understood, audited and handed over.
items.evidence: Completed model card and data sheet per system, version-controlled, covering intended use, limits, training data provenance and evaluation results.
items.test: Could an auditor who has never seen the system reconstruct what it does and why from the documentation alone?

items.description: Test models for bias across relevant groups, disaggregated rather than in aggregate, and act on what you find.
items.evidence: Fairness test plan with defined groups and thresholds; disaggregated results; remediation log for findings.
items.test: Are results reported per group, and is there a written threshold that would block release?
items.more: Australia AI6 practice 2 (impacts, incl. fairness); IEEE 2863-2026 (ethical principles)

items.description: Set the level of explanation each system must provide based on the risk and impact of its decisions, including to affected people.
items.evidence: Explainability standard by risk tier; sample explanations; human review and challenge route for affected individuals.
items.test: If a person asks why the system decided against them, what exactly do you send them, and who sends it?
items.euaiact: Art. 13, 14, 86 (transparency, human oversight, right to explanation)
items.more: Australia AI6 practices 4 and 6 (information for affected people; human control)

items.description: Protect data, models and outputs with security and privacy safeguards, including AI-specific threats such as prompt injection and data leakage.
items.evidence: Privacy impact assessment; AI threat model; red-team or penetration test results; access controls on training data and prompts.
items.test: Has the system been attacked on purpose (prompt injection, data exfiltration) before go-live, and were the findings fixed?
items.more: ISO/IEC 27090:2026 (AI security threats: poisoning, evasion, model inversion and extraction, prompt and output injection)

items.description: Monitor performance, data drift, fairness and system behaviour in production, with alerts that reach a named person.
items.evidence: Monitoring dashboard; defined metrics and thresholds; alert routing; drift and performance reports over time.
items.test: If accuracy dropped 10% after a vendor model update, who would get the alert, and how fast?
items.more: EN 18286:2026 (Art. 17(1)(h) post-market monitoring); Australia AI6 practice 5 (monitoring); ISO/IEC 27090:2026 (attack detection)

items.description: Define how AI incidents are detected, escalated, contained, remediated and reported, and rehearse it.
items.evidence: AI incident playbook; severity definitions; incident log; at least one tabletop exercise with lessons learned.
items.test: Can you switch the system off or roll it back today, and has anyone practised doing it?
items.more: EN 18286:2026 (Art. 17(1)(i) serious-incident procedures); Australia AI6 practice 5 (incident thresholds)

items.description: Track changing laws and standards and run periodic compliance assessments and independent audits.
items.evidence: Regulatory horizon register; compliance assessment schedule; internal audit reports and management responses.
items.test: When did a law affecting your AI last change, and how long did it take you to notice?
items.more: EN 18286:2026 (cited in the OJ on 14 Oct 2026; Art. 17(2)–(4) not covered); Australian Standards for AI (announced Jul 2026; legislation expected early 2027)

items.description: Set clear rules for safe, responsible and compliant use of generative AI tools and models, including approved tools and data limits.
items.evidence: Generative AI standard; approved-tools list; data classification rules for prompts; output review and labelling requirements.
items.test: Do staff know which tools are approved, and what data they must never paste into them?
items.euaiact: Art. 50 (transparency for certain AI systems), Art. 53 (GPAI providers)
items.more: ISO/IEC 27090:2026 (prompt injection; sensitive information in outputs)
